l: Jewish religion, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: The unit portrays Jewish religious and communal life through Passover, Tabernacle, and wedding festivals, Sabbath observance, and Jewish marriage customs. It also states that Jews in Mahometan countries were occasionally permitted to have four wives.

l: religion of the Atlas Jews, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: The religion of the Atlas Jews is described as differing from that of Jews generally: they are said to resemble Caraaites, to be unacquainted with Ezra or Christ, and to call the Supreme Being Shadai. Their written law is said to omit the deluge, describe distinct human species, and recount God's appearance to Ishmael.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: The Atlas Mountains shelter the main population of Shelouh Jews, especially around Jebel Melge, described as a vast ridge capped with eternal snows. The mountain setting is associated with their physical strength, isolation, independence, and freedom.

l: Tangier, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: Tangier had Jewish residents who sometimes returned from Gibraltar wearing European dress. The Emperor ordered such Jews to be undressed and to resume wearing the black turban so they could not pass as Christians or Europeans.

l: French bombardment of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: The French bombardment of Tangier and Mogador brought severe suffering to the Jewish communities. Jews were massacred or buried beneath ruins, their wives were plundered, and survivors wandered naked and starving or hid in the mountains.

l: Mogador sack and destruction, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: The plunder of Mogador was carried out from within while French forces attacked from outside. Moorish rabble targeted Jewish houses and women, while Berbers and Arabs later plundered both Jews and Moors who had escaped with booty.

l: Jewish polygamy, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: Jewish polygamy is portrayed as rare and disorderly. One Jewish silk-merchant in Tunis had four wives whose household was marked by rivalry, quarrelling, neglect of the older wives, and the overattention of all four women to their only child.

l: early marriage, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: Early marriage is common in the unit's account of Mogador, with girls sometimes married at nine and commonly at ten or eleven. A nine-year-old girl was reportedly married to a man over fifty.

l: marriage customs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: Marriage customs among Jews and Moors are presented as arrangements of sale and barter rather than love. Engagements may be broken over the value of household goods, and wealthy older men are said to be preferred over handsome and amiable young men.

l: female beauty and obesity, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: Jewish women are described as often having fair complexions, delicate features, and expressive eyes, while Moorish standards value extreme size in the lower back, thighs, calves, and knees. Betrothed women may be deliberately fattened with paste and prevented from exercising, and enormous women are treated as especially attractive.

l: white brandy, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
s: White brandy is described as a stimulant of immorality and intoxication in Moroccan society. Jews are said to produce and distribute it despite government punishment, while Moors drink it on the understanding that it is not grape juice, and Jewish families become excited and troubled by it on the Sabbath.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: The unit traces the succession of Maroquine dynasties from the Edristees in 789 through the Shereefs, who have ruled Morocco for more than three centuries. It describes the Shereefian genealogy and explains the dynasty’s descent from Ali and Fatima, the daughter of Mahomet. It profiles Muley Abd Errahman, who was selected by his uncle Muley Suleiman and strengthened imperial authority through frugal, conservative rule. It also discusses Morocco’s religious and political importance, the status of its Shereefs, and the limits of Abd-el-Kader’s ability to replace the reigning dynasty.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: Morocco is described as an immense remnant of the monarchies created by the Saracens and as the only remaining independent Mussulman kingdom founded by the Saracen conquest of North Africa. Its present Shereefian dynasty claims descent from the Prophet through Ali and Fatima and has ruled the country for more than three centuries.

l: Maroquine dynasties, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: The Maroquine dynasties are listed as the Edristees, Fatamites, Zuheirites, Moravedi, Almohades, Merinites, Oatagi, and Shereefs. They succeeded one another from the Edristee accession in 789 until the Shereefs became the reigning dynasty.

l: Shereefian dynasty, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: The Shereefian dynasty originated from a family near Medina in Arabia and gained control of Morocco through successive usurpations. It is divided into the Hoseinee branch and the El Fileli, or Tafilett, branch, with the latter forming the present ruling line.

l: Muley Abd Errahman, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: Muley Abd Errahman was chosen by his dying uncle, Muley Suleiman, instead of Suleiman’s own children. He is portrayed as a frugal and pacific ruler who consolidated imperial authority, preserved the empire through long periods of internal quiet, and generally avoided bloodshed, although he was accused of avarice, confiscations, and imprisonments.

l: Muley Suleiman, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: Muley Suleiman preferred his nephew Muley Abd Errahman as successor because Abd Errahman was considered more suitable to preserve and consolidate the empire. His designation of Abd Errahman was presented as an act of justice because Abd Errahman had been excluded from the succession earlier on account of his youth.

l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: The Shereefs are presented as descendants of the Prophet’s family and as profoundly venerated by true Mussulmen. Many members of the royal family reside at Tafilett, and the Shereefs there are described as living in a small fortified town in moderate or impoverished circumstances.

l: Islam, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: The Shereefian sultans are portrayed as religious leaders whose claim to head Islam is stronger than that of the Ottoman sultans, according to the text. The Shereefs’ descent from Ali and Fatima is said to give them exceptional authority among Mussulmen.

l: Abd-el-Kader, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: Abd-el-Kader is described as a highly revered marabout warrior and an object of enthusiasm among Mussulmen in North Africa, especially Morocco. The text argues that he could not have successfully dethroned the Shereefian emperor because Moroccans would not deliberately abandon the Prophet’s line for a ruler of different blood.

l: Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: Tafilett is identified as the ancient country of the Sherfah, or Shereefs, and as a place especially appropriated for members of the royal family. The present Shereefian branch extended its authority from Tafilett over the provinces of Morocco.

l: North Africa, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: North Africa is described as the region conquered by the Saracens and as the area where Abd-el-Kader was widely revered. Morocco is distinguished from Tunis and Tripoli, which are described as regencies, and from Algeria, which had become an integral part of France.

l: Moorish imperial throne, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
s: The Moorish imperial throne passed through a succession of dynasties before being held by the Shereefs. Muley Abd Errahman occupied it after Muley Suleiman and is credited with making imperial authority more solid and preserving the empire during his reign.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The unit recounts the succession crisis after Sidi Mohammed’s death, the reigns of Yezeed, Muley Hisham, and Muley Suleiman, and Muley Abd Errahman’s succession among the Shereefs. It praises Muley Suleiman’s peaceful rule and abolition of Christian slavery, while discussing Morocco’s relations with France, England, and Europe. It examines the slave trade and the Shereefian justification of it under Islam. It also criticizes the British-Moroccan treaties, especially their provisions for disputes involving British subjects, and describes British influence in Morocco, including at Gibraltar and Mogador.

l: Muley Suleiman, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Muley Suleiman was proclaimed Sultan in the north at Fez during the civil war following Yezeed’s death, and later became Sultan of the whole empire after Muley Hisham’s retirement. He is described as a good and patriotic prince who maintained peace and tranquility, remained neutral during European wars, cultivated peace with Europe, and abolished Christian slavery in his States. He died on 28 March 1820 after declaring his nephew, Muley Abd Errahman, his legitimate and hereditary successor.

l: Yezeed, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Yezeed was the hereditary prince and succeeded his father, Sidi Mohammed, three days after his death in April 1790 or 1789. He is portrayed as a tyrant whose cruelties caused civil war; he was mortally wounded by a poisoned arrow and died in February 1792 during the 22nd month of his reign. Despite his reputation, he was buried with great solemnities at the mosque of Kobah Sherfah because he was a Shereef.

l: Muley Hisham, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Muley Hisham disputed the succession after Yezeed’s death and was proclaimed Sultan in the south at Morrocco and Sous. In 1795 he retired to a sanctuary, where he soon died.

l: Muley Abd Errahman, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Muley Abd Errahman was declared by Muley Suleiman to be the legitimate and hereditary successor of the Shereefs. The text later describes him as pursuing a pacific policy with the assistance of his vizier, Bouseilam.

l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The Shereefs are presented as the lineage of Mussulman sovereigns claiming descent from the Prophets of God. Their rulers are described as exercising divine or inviolable Shereefian privileges, and the Shereefian Court defended slavery as authorized by Islamic scripture and tradition.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Morocco is described as an empire divided by civil war after Yezeed’s death and later governed by Muley Suleiman and Muley Abd Errahman. Its relations with European powers, especially England and France, are discussed through diplomacy, trade, piracy, slavery, and treaties.

l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Fez was the place where Muley Suleiman was saluted as Emperor in the north during the succession conflict. The text also refers to the war party and diplomatic activity at the Court of Fez.

l: Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The peace of Utrecht conceded Gibraltar to England, which the text says more than compensated England for the loss of Tangier. A treaty or arrangement also supplied provisions, especially cattle, to the garrison of Gibraltar.

l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Mogador is described as a place where European merchants, including Mr. Saferty, conducted business under the authority of the Moroccan government. The text says merchants there were sometimes prohibited from visiting vessels in or outside the port, despite a treaty provision appearing to permit it.

l: England, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: England’s influence and trade in Morocco expanded during the eighteenth century, and British influence was strengthened by the battle of Trafalgar and the fall of Napoleon. England concluded treaties with Morocco concerning peace, trade, piracy, and the treatment of British subjects.

l: France, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: France entered relations with the western Moors shortly after England and began sending its flag to Moroccan ports in 1555 under Francis I. France gained influence while England occupied Tangier, later sought a treaty of peace, and was associated with protection for a Jewish former consul who was decapitated by the Emperor.

l: Europe, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Muley Suleiman maintained neutrality while Christian powers in Europe were convulsed with war and cultivated peace with Europe. The text also discusses Morocco’s diplomatic intercourse with European princes and European efforts to influence Morocco.

l: Yezeed's succession crisis, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: After Sidi Mohammed’s death, Yezeed and Hisham disputed the succession, and Yezeed was proclaimed Sultan at Salee as the hereditary prince. Yezeed’s cruelties provoked civil war, and after his death the empire was divided among three pretenders before Muley Hisham and Muley Suleiman became the principal competitors.

l: Muley Suleiman's reign, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: Muley Suleiman’s reign lasted about a quarter of a century. The text characterizes it as peaceful and prosperous, noting his just administration, neutrality in European wars, peaceful relations with Europe, and abolition of Christian slavery.

l: abolition of Christian slavery, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The abolition of Christian slavery in Muley Suleiman’s States is identified as the most glorious and beneficent act of his reign from the perspective of European nations.

l: Christian slavery, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The text says that Moroccan rulers formerly subjected Christian captives to severe bondage, motivated partly by hostility toward Spain and revenge for injuries inflicted on the Moors. It credits Muley Suleiman with abolishing Christian slavery in his States.

l: slave trade, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The slave trade is defended in letters from the Sultan to Mr. Hay as a practice accepted since the time of the sons of Adam and confirmed by the Koran and the Sunnat. The correspondence states that Islamic law regulates the treatment, sale, emancipation, and religious transfer of slaves.

l: Islam, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The Shereefian correspondence presents Islam as authorizing slavery and the slave trade through the Koran and traditions of the Prophet. It also states that a Muslim, the sacred misshaf, and a young person may not be sold or given to an unbeliever.

l: Moorish law, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The British-Moroccan treaties provide that disputes involving British and Moorish subjects are to be decided according to Moorish law in specified circumstances. The text criticizes this arrangement because it could expose British subjects to punishments imposed under the Moorish legal system.

l: British influence in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: British influence in Morocco grew after the peace of Utrecht and was strengthened by Trafalgar and the fall of Napoleon. British diplomacy sought to support Muley Abd Errahman’s pacific policy, counter French influence, and prevent French pretexts for invading Morocco.

l: British-Moroccan treaties, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The principal treaty discussed was signed at Fez on 14 June 1801 and confirmed on 19 January 1824 by Muley Suleiman. It addressed consuls, trade, disputes, punishment, religious renegades, and access to vessels, but the text argues that it required immediate revision because it gave excessive authority to the Emperor and insufficient security to British subjects.

l: British subjects, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: British subjects in Morocco were granted treaty protections concerning consuls, commerce, disputes, punishment, and access to vessels. The text argues that they remained exposed to Moorish punishments and uncertain justice, citing the imprisonment and attempted punishment of Mr. Saferty at Mogador.

l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
s: The Moors are described as the inhabitants and rulers of Morocco, with historical conflicts involving England, France, Spain, and other European powers. The text says that Moors were subject to severe punishments under Moorish law and that disputes between Moors and Europeans were governed by the Moroccan authorities and treaties.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The unit describes the Empire of Morocco’s uncertain extent, military and commercial resources, political influence, geography, and population. It reviews the successive settlement and conquest of North Africa by Libyans, Getulians, Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Arabs, and distinguishes Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks among Morocco’s inhabitants. It explains that the Sultan’s authority is strong in religious and nominal terms but limited in many southern, northern, and mountainous regions. It also discusses Morocco’s natural boundaries, Atlas mountains, trade, and the mixed origins of its urban population.

l: Empire of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Empire of Morocco is presented as having either a restricted effective territory or a much wider sphere of nominal influence. Its dependent territory is estimated at about 137,400 square miles, while its population is approximately six million; its army, commerce, and authority over distant provinces are described as limited and uneven.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: Morocco is also called El-Gharb, or Mogrel-el-Aksa, meaning the West or Far West, and is sometimes called the Country of the Sultan Muley Abd Errahman. It is bounded by the Mediterranean and Straits of Gibraltar to the north, the Atlantic to the west, the Sahara and southern deserts to the south, and Algeria, the Atlas, and Tafilett to the east.

l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Sultan of Morocco is the head of the orthodox religion of the Mussulmen of the West and claims authority over territories where his direct power is often only nominal. He can use religious titles and honors, including those associated with the Shereefian Parasol, to set chiefs against one another and strengthen his position.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Atlas contains quasi-independent Berber tribes that oppose both the Arabs and the Moorish government. Its eastern and mountainous regions limit the Sultan’s authority, and some inhabitants of its snowy mountains are reported to have European-looking customs.

l: North Africa, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: North Africa is described as having been successively inhabited or conquered by Libyans, Getulians, Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Arabs. Its population is portrayed as religiously homogeneous under Islam, while its peoples include Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks.

l: Barbary, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: Barbary is the region in which the aboriginal tribes of North Africa were called Barbarians or Berbers by the Romans and Arabs. The term Barbary States derives from this designation.

l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Sahara forms Morocco’s southern boundary and contains distant oases over which the Shereefs formerly claimed, and sometimes still nominally claim, sovereignty. The oases of Touat, Agobli, and Taoudeni are described as having little or no effective dependence on Morocco.

l: Romans, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Romans took control of Africa from the Phoenicians or Carthaginians and encountered indigenous peoples whom they called Moors, Berbers, or Barbarians. After being displaced by the Vandals, they later expelled or destroyed the Vandals, but eventually lost North Africa to the Arabs.

l: Phoenicians, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Phoenicians successively invaded North Africa and established themselves on its shores around the foundation of Carthage, about 820 years before the Christian era. The Romans later received or wrested control of Africa from them.

l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Arabs invaded North Africa from Asia around the middle of the seventh century and fought both the Romans and the indigenous Berbers. Arabs later ruled Morocco and, after being expelled from Spain, many refugees settled in Barbary, contributing to the growth of maritime cities.

l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Berbers are presented as descendants or representatives of North Africa’s indigenous peoples, especially the Getulians, and as persistent opponents of foreign domination. They inhabit Morocco’s mountains, while many Arab tribes occupy the plains, and their resistance continued against Roman and Arab conquerors.

l: Berber race, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Berber race is described as including the Amayeegh and Shelouh varieties in Morocco. Its members are chiefly located in the mountains and are difficult to distinguish from Arabs or Moors when they adopt urban occupations, dress, or habits.

l: Moorish population, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Moorish population is concentrated mainly in Morocco’s towns and cities and consists of a mixture of many races, including descendants of Moors expelled from Spain. Europeans commonly call urban inhabitants Moors, although the population itself distinguishes more specifically between Arabs and Berber tribes.

l: Islam, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: Islam provides the common religion that helps hold Morocco’s diverse populations together. The Sultan’s religious position allows him to claim influence across Western Barbary and Central Africa wherever Muslims are found, and a Christian or other non-Muslim enemy could unite otherwise hostile tribes.

l: Arab conquest of North Africa, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The Arab conquest of North Africa began around 650, when Arab forces from Asia attacked the declining Roman power. The Berbers initially submitted to the Arabs to escape Roman rule, then revolted and continued the struggle against their new conquerors.

l: Arab conquest of Spain, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
s: The conquering Arabs crossed from North Africa into Spain in the early eighth century. Because they came from Mauritania, the Spaniards called them Moors, although the text states that they may have had little in common with the indigenous Moors of North Africa.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: The unit describes Morocco’s climate, geography, agriculture, commerce, mineral resources, and animal life. It compares Morocco’s soil and climate with those of Spain and Portugal and identifies the Atlas Mountains as its dominant geographic feature. Morocco produces grain, fruits, vegetables, timber, and regionally distinctive argan oil, while its northern and southern regions export different staple goods. The unit also reports that Morocco possesses extensive but largely neglected mineral resources and describes the desert horse called sherb-errech.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: Morocco is described as one of the healthiest countries in Africa, except perhaps Tunis, because of its Atlantic exposure, Atlas elevations, varied terrain, and lack of extensive marshes. Its surface consists largely of a central ridge with slopes toward the Atlantic and the Sahara, and its coasts have few well-protected ports.

l: Atlantic Ocean, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: The Atlantic Ocean borders Morocco to the west and receives the country’s northwestern rivers. The Atlantic coast is characterized mainly by ridges of hills, and its ports offer poor protection from the ocean.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: The Atlas Mountains traverse Morocco from northeast to southwest, and their highest stated point, Miltsin, rises more than 15,000 feet above sea level. The mountains influence Morocco’s climate, produce numerous rivers, and contain forests, mineral resources, and the highest peaks of the Moroccan portion of the range.

l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: The Sahara receives the southeastern slopes and streams of Morocco, including waters that feed the Wad Draha and other rivers before disappearing into desert sands. Southern Morocco has more desert heat and less rain because of its proximity to the Sahara.

l: Elaeonderron Argan, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: Eloeondenron Argan is a tree peculiar to southern Morocco. Its fruit resembles an olive and contains an almond whose crushed kernel produces a rancid oil commonly used instead of olive oil.

l: Argan, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: Argan trees are bushy and large, sometimes reaching the size of wide-spreading oaks. Several argan forests grow near Mogador.

l: climate and soil of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: The climate and soil of Morocco are described as similar to those of Spain and Portugal. Northern Morocco has a climate nearly like Spain’s, while the south has less rain and more desert heat but greater fertility for valuable commercial staples.

l: agriculture of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: Agriculture centers on wheat and barley in the plains, while vegetables and fruits are cultivated near towns. Irrigation sustains cultivation when rains cease or fail, allowing Southern European fruits and vegetables, as well as plants suited to Africa, to be grown successfully.

l: Moroccan commerce, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: Northern Morocco exports cattle, grain, bark, leeches, and skins, while southern Morocco exports gums, almonds, ostrich feathers, wax, wool, and skins. Cork, salt, argan oil, leather-related plants, and fish such as the Shebbel also contribute to commerce.

l: Moroccan mineral resources, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
s: Morocco possesses deposits of gold, silver, lead, iron, tin, sulphur, mineral salt, antimony, copper, saltpetre, and amethyst. Most mines are neglected or unworked because the government fears encouraging foreign interest, although silver mines in Sous, copper mines between several southern settlements, and other deposits are identified.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The unit describes Morocco’s political, tribal, and natural divisions, distinguishing the northern Rif, the central Atlas, and the southern quasi-Saharan region. It questions the reliability of Moroccan population statistics and surveys coastal towns, ports, and Spanish presidios along the Mediterranean. Particular attention is given to the Jafarine Isles, Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, Gomera, Tetouan, and Ceuta, including their populations, strategic positions, commerce, and relations with Spain. It also describes the Berbers of the Rif and Garet and recounts Abd-el-Kader’s refuge among them.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Morocco is described as having historically been divided into the kingdoms or provinces of Morocco and Fez, with Tafilett and sometimes Sous attached to Morocco. Its modern divisions include northern Fez, central Morocco, eastern Tafilett, and southern Sous, while its practical administration is based chiefly on tribes and kaidats. Its coastal towns, interior regions, and natural resources are surveyed, although reliable population information is difficult to obtain.

l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Fez was historically a powerful independent kingdom extending eastward to the gates of Tlemsen. In the modern geographical division it is identified with the northern kingdom of Fez and is listed among the districts of the central Atlas region.

l: Mulweeah, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Moulwia, also called Mulweeah or Malwia, forms an important reference point for Morocco’s northern coast. The Rif is described as extending from the river’s mouth toward Tangier, and the Jafarine Isles lie near its mouth; Kalat-el-wad is situated near the river, although its navigability is unknown.

l: Rif, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Rif is Morocco’s mountainous northern coastal region, extending along the Mediterranean from the Moulwia to Tangier. It contains the districts of Hashbat, Gharet, and Aklaia and is inhabited by warlike Berbers over whom the Sultan exercises precarious authority. The region is fertile and mineral-rich, with cork forests, grazing valleys, and exports of skins, but travel there is described as exceptionally dangerous.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Atlas is presented as Morocco’s central great mountain chain, called the Deren by the natives, extending from the Algerian frontier to Cape Gheer. It separates the northern regions from the southern quasi-Saharan region and includes or borders districts such as Fez, Morocco, Todla, Dukala, Abda, Haha, and Sous.

l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Sahara is included in the quasi-Saharan region south of the Atlas, particularly in the area southeast of the mountain chain. The text treats the Sahara as a comparison for the dangers of travel in the Rif, stating that travel in the Rif is more dangerous than in the farthest wastes of the Sahara.

l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Berbers inhabit the provinces of Rif and Garet and are portrayed as warlike, semi-barbarous, and only loosely controlled by the Sultan. They graze herds and flocks in the Rif’s valleys, exploit its forests and resources, and participate in fierce disputes at market gatherings.

l: Spanish, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Spanish possess the Jafarine Isles and the presidios of Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, and Ceuta on the Moroccan coast. Their settlements are described as fortified or penal establishments, and their authority is portrayed as a remnant of Spain’s weakened power.

l: Abd-el-Kader, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Abd-el-Kader sought refuge and support among the tribes of the Rif after withdrawing from Algeria. He resisted the Imperial government there for several months but ultimately chose to confront the Sultan in a pitched battle.

l: Jafarine Isles, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Jafarine Isles are three islands near the mouth of the Moulwia that belong to Spain. They had recently been additionally fortified, although the text questions the purpose of those fortifications; a small town is said to stand on the mainland opposite them.

l: Melilla, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Melilla, an ancient Carthaginian city near the cape called Rusadir by the Romans, is the capital of Garet and is said to contain about 3,000 inhabitants. It lies amid fertile country rich in minerals and honey. A nearby Spanish presidio, also called Melilla, occupies an island connected to the mainland by a drawbridge and is reported to contain 2,244 people by Spanish figures, though other writers give a lower number.

l: Garet, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Garet is a northern Moroccan province containing Melilla and extending through a rich and highly cultivated region. Like the Rif, it is inhabited by warlike Berbers over whom the Sultan’s authority is precarious.

l: Alhucemas, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Alhucemas is a small Spanish island presidio containing approximately five or six hundred inhabitants. It commands the bay of the same name at the mouth of the Wad Nechor, near the Islet of Ed-Housh; the ruined ancient capital of Mezemma lies nearby.

l: Penon de Velez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Penon de Velez is a Spanish presidio island and convict settlement situated opposite the mouths of the Gomera River. It is a strong position with a garrison and population of about nine hundred, but it is largely a barren rock and must receive fresh water from the mainland for part of the year.

l: Gomera, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Gomera, or Badis, lies on the mainland opposite Penon de Velez and is identified with several ancient names, including Parientina and possibly the Acra of Ptolemy. Although Count Graberg claimed that it contained 3,000 inhabitants, other and later writers described it as abandoned and inhabited only by serpents and hyenas.

l: Tetouan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Tetouan, identified with the Roman Yagath, is a large, prosperous, and commercial city of the province of Hasbat, situated several miles inland from the Mediterranean. It has gardens, olive and vine plantations, extensive orange groves, covered bazaars, a Jewish quarter, and a nearby port at Marteen or Marteel. Its population is variously estimated at 9,000 to 12,000, and its fortifications are strong enough mainly to resist hostile Berbers.

l: Tangier, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Tangier marks the western extent of the Rif in the unit’s description of the northern coast. Tetouan lies roughly two-thirds of a day’s journey southeast of Tangier, and the northern intermediate zone extends from Tangier toward Mogador.

l: Ceuta, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Ceuta, or Sebta, is an ancient city and fortress identified with Esilissa of Ptolemy and formerly regarded as the capital of Mauritania Tingitana. Portugal conquered it in 1415, and Spain retained it after Portugal recovered its independence in 1640. It contains a Spanish garrison of roughly 2,000 to 3,000 men, a free population of about 5,000 to 6,000, and a small insecure port.

l: Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Gibraltar is described as lying opposite Ceuta across the Straits of Gibraltar and as the European counterpart of the African Pillars of Hercules. The text also mentions the supposed subterranean passage beneath the straits through which monkeys were fancifully believed to travel between Gibraltar and Africa.

l: Straits of Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Straits of Gibraltar are the maritime setting of Ceuta, which stands fourteen miles south of Gibraltar and nearly opposite it. The surrounding mountains are identified with the African Pillars of Hercules, facing Gibraltar as the European pillar.

l: Spain's North African presidios, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Spain's North African presidios include the settlements at Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, and Ceuta, as well as the fortified Jafarine Isles. They are characterized as garrisons or convict settlements established on islands, peninsulas, or coastal strongpoints, and the text calls them of limited utility apart from their military or penal functions.

l: population statistics of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Moroccan population statistics are described as approximate and conjectural because local people resist counting populations and regard such questions as ill-omened, intrusive, or suggestive of espionage. Conflicting estimates for Mazagran, Melilla, Gomera, and other places are offered as evidence of their unreliability. The text nevertheless attempts to provide figures to indicate Morocco’s approximate strength and resources.

l: Moroccan coastal towns and ports, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Moroccan coastal towns and ports on the Mediterranean are said to be important but poorly documented, apart from the Spanish presidios and well-known places such as Tetouan and Tangier. The unit describes Kalat-el-wad, Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, Gomera, Tegaza, Tetouan, and Ceuta, noting their trade, fortifications, populations, bays, and varying degrees of accessibility.

l: Moroccan tribal administration, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
s: Moroccan tribal administration is presented as more fundamental than European-style provincial divisions. Districts and mountains are commonly named after their chief tribes, while kaidats provide a jurisdictional structure more comparable to European government. The Sultan’s authority is especially weak among the Berber tribes of the Rif and Garet.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: The unit describes towns, rivers, tribes, fortifications, populations, commerce, and historical events along Morocco's Atlantic coast, from Arzila southward to Mogador. It discusses Arzila, El Araish, Mehedia, Salee, Rabat, Fidallah, Dar-el-Beida, Azamor, Mazagran, Saffee, and El-Waladia, including their ports and relations with Portuguese, Spanish, Moorish, and European powers. It also connects ancient sites such as Lixus and Shella with Roman, Phoenician, Carthaginian, and Berber history. The text highlights the activities of the Salee rovers and the historical importance of Almanzor and the Bouragrag River.

l: Arzila, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Arzila, or Asila, is an ancient Berber city in the province of Hasbat, formerly called Zilia and Zulia by the Romans. It lies on the naked Atlantic shore, has a small port, a population of about one thousand, and produces good tobacco; its Portuguese fortifications are rapidly decaying under Moorish possession.

l: Atlantic Ocean, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: The Atlantic Ocean borders the Moroccan towns described in this unit, including Arzila, El Araish, and the coastal settlements farther south. Its shores and roadsteads provide ports and anchorages, although many entrances are obstructed by sandbars, rocks, or shallow water.

l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: The Moors possess or govern many of the towns described, including Arzila, El Araish, Mehedia, Salee, Rabat, and Dar-el-Beida. They have retaken several coastal strongholds from the Portuguese or Spanish, but some Moorish fortifications and ports are described as weak, neglected, or decaying.

l: El Araish, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: El Araish, also called Laratsh, replaces the ancient city of Lixus and is the capital and seat of the governor of the district of Azgar. It has a population of about four thousand according to one estimate, a garrison of five hundred troops, a difficult port on the river Cos or Luccos, and exports cork, wool, skins, bark, beans, and grain.

l: Azgar, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Azgar is the district whose capital and governor's residence is El Araish. Its name is connected in the text with a powerful tribe of the Touaricks, and its environs include the Beni-Arous vineyards and the Beni Arasis mountains.

l: Lixus, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Lixus, also called Liscas and Lixa, was the ancient city replaced by El Araish. Its Phoenician coins depict grapes, ears of corn, and fishes, reflecting the area's vineyards, grain fields, and rivers.

l: Mauritania, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Mauritania is described through the ancient Roman frontier and the fertile Atlantic region associated with Lixus. Strabo characterizes most of it as rich, fertile, well watered, and abundant in trees and other products, while Salee is identified as the farthest Roman city on the Atlantic coast of ancient Mauritania Tingitana.

l: Mehedia, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Mehedia, also called Mamora or Nuova Mamora, stands near the mouth of the Sebou on the edge of the Mamora plain and forest. It was captured by the Spaniards in 1614 and retaken by the Moors in 1681; it later became a weak settlement with fishermen, a small garrison, and a crumbling castle.

l: Salee, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Salee, or Sala, is an ancient city on the right bank of the Bouragrag near its mouth and a major commercial and fortified city of Beni-Hassan. It was captured by Alphonso the Wise in 1263, returned to Moorish rule, and later became a center of piracy; its population estimates vary widely, and Christians and Jews were not permitted to reside there.

l: Bouragrag River, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: The Bouragrag River flows between Salee on its right bank and Rabat on its left bank before reaching the Atlantic. It is broad near the two cities and is presented as a natural line separating the more humid northern side from the higher and drier southern side.

l: Salee rovers, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: The Salee rovers were Moroccan pirates based at Salee and Rabat who formed a nearly independent military republic. They were described as exceptionally ferocious and courageous and once operated as far away as Lundy Island in the British Channel.

l: Rabat, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Rabat, or Er-Rabat, is a large, densely populated, fortified city opposite Salee on the Bouragrag River. It was built by Yakob-el-Mansour as Rabat-el-Fatah, contains wealthy Jewish residents and active merchants, and has gardens, plantations, forts, and a mausoleum associated with Almanzor.

l: Jakoub Almanzor, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Almanzor, also called Elmansor, was a famous and victorious Sultan who intended Rabat to be his capital. The text says that he expelled the Moravedi from Spain and that his untenanted mausoleum stands in Rabat.

l: Dar-el-Beida, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Dar-el-Beida, or Casa-Blanco, is a small Atlantic town built by the Portuguese on the ruins of Anafa, which they destroyed in 1468. It has a small port and a spacious bay capable of sheltering large vessels, but its population is estimated at only about one thousand or as few as two hundred.

l: Azamor, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Azamor, or Azemmour, is an ancient Berber city of Dukaila whose name means olives in the Berber language. It lies near the mouth of the Omm-er-Rbia, has fertile surroundings and a trade in Shebbel salmon, and was captured and fortified by the Portuguese in 1513 before being abandoned about a century later.

l: Mazagran, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Mazagran is an ancient and strong castle on a peninsula at the bottom of a spacious bay, rebuilt by the Portuguese in 1506 as Castillo Real. The Portuguese abandoned it in 1769, making it their last stronghold in Morocco; it has thick walls, a small port, and a population of two or three hundred.

l: Saffee, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Saffee, properly Asafee and formerly Soffia or Saffia, is an ancient city of Abda built by the Carthaginians near Cape Pantin. It has massive walls, a summer roadstead, and a history of European commerce, but its population is about one thousand and the surrounding country is comparatively uncultivated.

l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
s: Mogador is mentioned as the next destination after the description of El-Waladia. The text states that Mogador and Aghadir have already been described.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The unit describes the imperial cities of Morocco, El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco, as well as Tafilett, the birthplace of the ruling Shereefian dynasty. It records their locations, populations, defenses, religious and commercial institutions, historical origins, and apparent decline. Fez is presented as the Empire’s principal center of learning and commerce, Mequinez as a fortified royal residence and treasury, Morocco as the southern capital, and Tafilett as a caravan mart and place associated with the Imperial family. The account concludes that the cities and the wider Moorish civilization are declining and may require reconstruction by European hands.

l: Imperial Cities of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Imperial Cities of Morocco are identified as El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco. They are described as royal or capital cities with important roles in administration, defense, commerce, religion, and learning, although all are said to be in decline.

l: Empire of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Maroquine Empire contains the royal cities of El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco, together with Tafilett and its surrounding districts. Its principal cities are portrayed as politically divided, commercially active, and weakened by decay and inadequate defenses.

l: El-Kesar, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: El-Kesar lies in the province of the Gharb on the southern bank of the Luccos. It was enlarged and beautified by Almansor around 1180 as a military magazine and rendezvous, but its narrow streets, ruined houses, inactive mosques, and small population reflect decline. The Battle of the Three Kings took place there in 1578.

l: Battle of the Three Kings, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Battle of the Three Kings occurred at El-Kesar in 1578. Don Sebastian, the Portuguese king, and two Moorish princes perished in connection with the battle, while Muley Moluc died secretly in a litter so that the Moorish forces would not lose courage.

l: Mequinez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Mequinez, or Miknas, is a royal residence and city of the province of Fez, situated on a hill in a well-watered and pleasant region. It is surrounded by a triple wall, contains much of the Imperial guard, and holds royal treasures estimated at about fifty million dollars. Its inhabitants are described as polished, kind, and hospitable, while its palace is noted for elaborate stucco Arabesque work.

l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Berbers founded Mequinez through the tribe of Meknasab, a fraction of the Zenatah, in the middle of the tenth century. Berbers also inhabit the mountains near Mequinez and are among the peoples whose revolts or disaffection concern the Sultan.

l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Fez is described as one of the leading cities of Morocco in learning, wealth, industry, commerce, and religious importance. It contains old and new sections, hundreds of mosques, schools, markets, caravans, and manufactures, but its walls and defenses are decayed and its inhabitants are characterized as fanatical. Its population is uncertain, with estimates ranging from about thirty thousand to eighty-eight thousand or more.

l: Edris-Ben-Edris, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Edris-Ben-Edris inherited the virtues and influence of his father, Edris Ben Abdalluh. He is credited with being the first bona-fide Mussulman sovereign of the Maroquine empire and with founding Fez.

l: El-Karoubin, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: El-Karoubin, also called El-Karouiin, is the most famous mosque of Fez and is supported by three hundred pillars. It is said to contain a celebrated ancient library with Greek and Latin authors and lost books of Titus Livy, although the text treats this claim as conjectural.

l: Muley Edris, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Muley Edris is identified as the founder of the modern city of Fez, whose ashes rest in a revered mosque mausoleum. The people are said to invoke his name in prayers, treating him with excessive veneration.

l: Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Tafilett consists of fortified towns and villages on the south-eastern side of the Atlas and is inhabited partly by the Imperial family. It is a major caravan rendezvous and market for products from the surrounding countries and the Sahara. The area is also used as a place of exile for troublesome members of the Imperial family.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Morocco, or Maraksh, is the capital of the South and is sometimes called the capital of the Empire, though it is described as a diminished shadow of its former greatness. It has extensive walls, mosques, markets, gardens, an Imperial palace, and caravan trade, but its streets and buildings are decayed and its learning is limited. Its population estimates range from about thirty thousand to one hundred thousand.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Atlas lies near Morocco, whose city spreads across a plain at its foot. The Atlas supplies water through streams and aqueducts and forms the geographical setting for Tafilett on its south-eastern side.

l: Eastern Province of Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Tafilett province was anciently called Sedjelmasa and later took the name Tafilett from an Arab immigrant associated with improved date cultivation. It contains several fortified towns and fertile level districts producing corn, fruits, vegetables, sheep, and woollen and silk manufactures.

l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Shereefs are descendants or family members of the Prophet and inhabit Tafilett, which is called the country of the Shereefs. The ruling family is described as a southern African branch of Shereefs rather than Shereefs of Fez.

l: Shereefian dynasty, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The present dynasty belongs to Morocco and is identified as a dynasty of Shereefs from the south. Its rulers must favor Fez at times to maintain the allegiance of the northern country, while the dynasty’s authority is threatened by restless tribes and rival political centers.

l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: The Sultan of Morocco resides mainly at Fez, Mequinez, and Morocco, using his presence to maintain allegiance and restrain disaffected tribes. He sends troublesome members of his family to Tafilett, and he sometimes retreats to Morocco when relations with European powers become difficult. The text says that the Emperors never visit Tafilett except as dethroned exiles.

l: France, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: France is mentioned in connection with hostilities provoked by the fanatics of Fez and with the possibility of awakening the population’s energies. The text suggests that European intervention, including that of France, might help reconstruct the declining royal cities.

l: Moorish civilization, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
s: Moorish civilization is portrayed as having entered a period of decline, with ruined cities, decaying fortifications, diminished learning, and weakened institutions. The text calls the royal cities the remnants of a once flourishing civilization and suggests that they may not recover without European reconstruction.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit describes towns, cities, rivers, provinces, tribes, and trade routes in Morocco, especially the Kingdom of Fez and the southern regions of Sous, Draha, and Tafilett. It discusses places including Wazen, Muley Driss, Taza, Oushda, Aghmat, and many smaller settlements, noting their populations, commerce, agriculture, fortifications, and political organization. The text emphasizes the influence and near-independence of Amazirgh, Berber, and Shelouh communities, as well as the economic importance of Jews in many towns. It concludes by questioning existing population estimates and describing the uncertainty surrounding the interior geography of Morocco.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit surveys Morocco's interior towns and cities, including regions of the Kingdom of Fez, Sous, Draha, and Tafilett. It describes Morocco as politically weakened by independent or semi-independent tribes and as having poorly documented geography and population.

l: Northern kingdom of Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Kingdom of Fez includes places such as Seisouan, Wazen, Muley Driss, Taza, Oushda, Aghla, Nakhila, and Meshra Khaluf. Its districts contain fertile plains, commercial towns, sanctuaries, and areas where local religious or tribal authorities exercise considerable independence.

l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Fez is used as a point of reference for the distances of several towns, including Muley Driss, Dubdu, Taza, Oushda, and Aghla. The surrounding kingdom is described as containing important commercial and agricultural districts.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Atlas range is associated with picturesque mountain scenery, Berber settlements, fertile valleys, and routes toward the southern provinces. Several towns, including Tefza, Pitideb, Ghuer, and Tednest, are situated on or near its mountains.

l: Wazen, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Wazen, in the province of Azgar and the region of the Gharb, is a small city without walls and the residence of the hereditary High Priest or Grand Marabout. Its religious ruler exercises substantial influence, and the district pays no tribute to the imperial government.

l: Muley Driss, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Muley Driss, also called Zawiat-Muley-Driss or Muley Edris, is a renowned city in the province of Fez at the foot of the mountains of Terhoun. It contains a sanctuary dedicated to Edris, founder of the Edrisiti dynasty, and lies in a fertile country producing many necessities and luxuries.

l: Taza, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Taza is the capital of the well-watered district of Haiaina and is described as one of the finest cities in Morocco. Built on a rock surrounded by a river, it has spacious streets, a large mosque, good provisions, hospitable inhabitants, and commerce with Tlemsen and Fez.

l: Oushda, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Oushda is a frontier town in the northeast, protected by a fortress and enclosed by garden walls. Its small population lives among low clay houses and winding streets, while irrigated gardens produce melons, olives, and figs; the surrounding Desert of Angad is extremely arid, especially in summer.

l: Sous, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sous is a southern region containing towns such as Tagawost, Fedsi, Messa or Assah, Talent, and Shtouka. It has fertile areas, trade with the Sahara and Timbuctoo, divisions among Shelouhs, Moors, and Jews, and districts that are sometimes nearly independent of Morocco.

l: Draha, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Draha is a southern province containing Beni-Sabih, Tatta, and Akka, with caravan routes leading toward the Great Desert. Beni-Sabih, also called Moussabal or Draha, is its small but populated and commercial capital.

l: Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Tafilett is identified as a southern destination reached by the road from Aghmat. The unit includes it among the distinguished places of Morocco but provides little further description.

l: Amazirghs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Amazirghs are described as an aboriginal population with their own elders, chiefs, and local institutions. Their mountain tribes frequently resist imperial authority, and their leaders may exploit conflicts between Morocco and European powers to avenge old grievances.

l: Omm-er-Rbia River, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Omm-Erbegh River passes near or through several settlements, including Meshra Khaluf, Tijijet, Bulawan, Soubeit, and Meramer. It provides fords and routes of travel, and the surrounding districts are often fertile and productive in grain and cattle.

l: Aghmat, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aghmat was formerly a great fortified city and the capital of Rhamna, but it has declined into a village inhabited by about sixty families, including a few Jews. It lies near the Atlas and a river of the same name in a fertile country of orchards and vineyards, and it was the first capital of the Marabout dynasty.

l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Sahara begins beyond the Mulweeah, more than forty leagues from Tlemsen, and is described as extremely sterile, particularly in summer. Tatta and Akka serve as meeting points for caravans crossing the Great Desert.

l: Berber race, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Shelouhs are presented as a major Berber population in the southern towns and districts, whose presence is suggested by the frequent use of names beginning or ending with the letter T. They inhabit places such as Dimenet, Fronga, and Tagawost, and often trade or live alongside Moors and Jews.

l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Berbers built or inhabited many of the towns described, including Tefza, Pitideb, Meramer, Tednest, Aghmat, and Messa. The text portrays them as an aboriginal population whose mountain communities often retain substantial political independence.

l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Arabs appear among the mixed and nomadic populations of Morocco and inhabit or visit many of the described districts. The author argues that previous writers have overstated their numbers relative to the aboriginal Amazirgh population.

l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Moors are described as inhabitants of towns such as Oushda, Messa or Assah, and Akka, and as part of the mixed population estimates for Morocco. The text distinguishes them from Arabs in some demographic classifications and notes that many people called Moors may descend from aboriginal Amazirghs.

l: Jews, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Jews are present in many towns as merchants, artisans, traders, and sometimes farmers. The unit repeatedly describes Jewish quarters or populations in places such as Tefza, Tagodast, Dimenet, Tednest, Akka, Messa, and Ilirgh, and argues that Jewish commerce is important to the economic life of North African Muslims.

l: Graeberg de Hemso, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Graeberg supplies population figures and descriptions for many Moroccan towns. The author considers his total estimate of 8,500,000 exaggerated but more moderate than Jackson's, suggesting that deducting two million may produce a more probable figure.

l: population statistics of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit questions the reliability of Moroccan population statistics because the towns enumerated appear to contain scarcely one million inhabitants and the tribal population is poorly known. Graeberg estimates 8,500,000 people, while the author considers a total reduced by about two million more plausible and rejects Jackson's estimate of nearly fifteen million as excessive.

l: interior geography of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: The interior geography of Morocco, particularly in the south, is described as obscure, with multiple names and uncertain locations appearing on maps. The author selects places whose existence is considered certain while acknowledging discrepancies between sources such as Graeberg and Davidson.

l: Moroccan tribal independence, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
s: Many Moroccan districts and tribes operate with substantial independence from the Sultan. Religious leaders at Wazen and Tedda, Amazirgh chiefs, and communities in places such as Talent and Shtouka may collect no imperial tribute or govern themselves with only nominal submission to Morocco.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: The Maroquine Sahara includes the oasis cluster of Figheegh, also called Figuiq, which consists of twelve villages. The villages lie along the descent of Wal-el-Khalouf and depend on wells and regulated water for their gardens, where date-palms, fruit trees, madder-root, tobacco, and barley are cultivated. The villages frequently fight over water, despite having commercial relations with Fez, Tafilett, and Touat. The people of Figheegh are generally prosperous through commerce, industry, and mining as well as agriculture.

l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: The Maroquine Sahara contains the oasis cluster of Figheegh, or Figuiq. Its settlements are described as a Saharan district with gardens, wells, agriculture, commerce, and mining.

l: Figheegh, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: Figheegh, also called Figuiq, is an agglomeration of twelve villages known for palm plantations and date production. It has commercial relations with Fez, Tafilett, and Touat, and its people are generally prosperous.

l: villages of Figheegh, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: The twelve villages are generally close together, no more than a quarter of a league apart, and lie on the descent of Wal-el-Khalouf. They have houses, mosques, schools, religious and civil leaders, crenated walls, and defensive towers; the larger villages include Maiz, El-Wadghir, and Zenega.

l: Wal-el-Khalouf, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: Wal-el-Khalouf, meaning "river of the wild boar," is dry except in winter. Its bed contains inexhaustible wells whose water is distributed to the gardens.

l: date-palm, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: Date-palms are abundant in the gardens of Figheegh, and their dates supply the western province of Algeria. The villages' wars are unusually destructive because the inhabitants destroy the fruitful palms, unlike communities elsewhere in the Sahara that spare them during bloodshed.

l: water, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: Water is obtained from wells in the bed of Wal-el-Khalouf and distributed among the gardens by means of a clepsydra, a vessel that releases a measured amount over an hour. Its scarcity and distribution are the immediate causes of discord among the villages.

l: strife among the villages, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: The villages are perpetually in conflict and sometimes take up arms against one another. Their wars are especially cruel, involving the destruction of productive date-palms, and water is identified as the immediate cause of their disputes.

l: people of Figheegh, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
s: The people of Figheegh cultivate madder-root, tobacco, barley, fruit trees, and date-palms, and they are skilled miners. Although they engage in severe warfare, they also practice commerce and various industries and are generally prosperous.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The narrator describes tensions involving London Jew-boys, Moors, and the British Consul at Mogador, including the imprisonment of a Jewish youth after he cursed a Moor. He visits Saneeates-Sultan, also called the Garden of the Emperor, and describes the barren landscape, the Argan tree, and legends of the Argan forests. In a further interview, the Governor of Mogador says that the Sultan of Morocco will not accept an anti-slavery appeal except under superior force. The narrator also records Moorish opinions that abolition might have gained more support through stronger official representation, gifts, or influence from Tunis and Constantinople.

l: London Jew-boys, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: London Jew-boys of the lower lemon-selling class are described as highly resentful of the contempt shown to them by the Moors. One was imprisoned by the British Consul after returning a Moor's curse.

l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Moors are said to treat London Jew-boys with contempt, and some reportedly wished that a fire at a Jewish merchant's house had spread so they could appropriate goods. The Governor says that most Moors oppose abolition, although some favor it.

l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: Mogador is the setting for disputes involving London Jew-boys, the British Consul, Jewish merchants, and the Governor. The narrator also distributed Arabic anti-slavery tracts and prepared an anti-slavery circular for British merchants there.

l: Saneeates-Sultan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: Saneeates-Sultan, three or four hours' ride south of Mogador, is visited by the narrator and companions. Its valley contains the Garden of the Emperor, the river Wad-el-Kesab, sandy mounds, palmettos, Argan trees, and little cultivated land.

l: Garden of the Emperor, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Garden of the Emperor contains a well, a few fruit trees, and a celebrated Argan tree. European visitors carved their names into the bark of a fine fig tree there.

l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: A great part of Morocco is described as having a desolate appearance, with uncultivated land and sparse vegetation. The narrator says that European visitors generally adopt Moorish habits rather than promoting Christian intellectual pleasures.

l: Argan forests, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Argan forests are associated with Moorish legends of enchantresses, magical springs, deceptive fruit, and wicked jinns. According to the tale, a holy man released the forests from enchantment by tying pieces of cork bark bearing the sacred name of the Deity to the trees.

l: Elaeonderron Argan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The narrator visits a celebrated, ancient Argan tree said by the people to have been planted by Okba. Its broad branches provide shade for many people, and the narrator compares its grandeur with the enchanted wood described by Tasso.

l: Governor of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Governor of Mogador tells the narrator that he has heard nothing improper about his conduct and regrets being unable to assist his anti-slavery work. He says the Sultan will not be persuaded on slavery by argument, though he jokes about his own slaves and asks the narrator what he would pay for them.

l: Mr. Treppass, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: Mr. Treppass accompanies the narrator to the interview with the Governor and assists with interpretation. He believes that a larger deputation carrying presents and official authority might have produced a better effect, and that many Moors favor abolition.

l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Governor says that the Sultan of Morocco will never listen to an appeal for abolition, even if presented by another official representative. He says the Sultan might yield only if Christians conquered the country and imposed the matter by superior force.

l: anti-slavery mission, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The anti-slavery mission sought to persuade the Sultan and Moroccan authorities to consider an address against slavery. The narrator is told that the mission might have appeared more effective with stronger official backing, several delegates, presents, and letters from the Bey of Tunis.

l: abolition of slavery, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Governor says that the Sultan will not accept abolition through persuasion, while Mr. Treppass believes that a considerable number of Moors support it. The narrator suggests that abolition by the Turkish Sultan could influence Morocco.

l: slavery, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Governor says that the Koran does not command the liberation of slaves, although it commends those who voluntarily free them. He acknowledges divisions among Muslims over the subject and says that most people in his community oppose abolition.

l: Bey of Tunis, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Bey of Tunis is cited as a Muslim ruler who has entered into engagements with Christians for the suppression of slavery. Moorish advisers say that letters showing what had been done in Tunis might have strengthened the narrator's mission.

l: Imaum of Muscat, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Imaum of Muscat is cited alongside the Bey of Tunis as a Muslim ruler who has entered into engagements with Christians for the suppression of slavery. The Governor explains that their views differ from those held in Morocco.

l: Koran, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Governor denies that the Koran commands the abolition of slavery. He says that it commends Muslims who voluntarily liberate their slaves and promises them God's blessing.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The unit describes El-Jereed, the Tunisian Sahara, its salt lake El-Sibhah, and its dependence on dates and the date-palm. It explains how date-palms are propagated, cultivated, irrigated, tapped for sap, and used for food, drink, building, and crafts. It also portrays palm-groves, date production and trade, and the importance of tribute collected by the Bey of the Camp. The unit concludes by introducing a forthcoming Tour to the Jereed, including accounts of Toser, Nefta, and Ghafsa.

l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: El-Jereed, or Belad-el-Jereed, is described as the country of dates and a part of the Sahara near the Great Desert. Its principal resources are dates and palm products, and about twenty thousand people live there for six months of the year entirely on dates. The region is an important part of the Tunisian territory and provides the Government with substantial revenue.

l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Sahara is described as the hot, dry country lying near the Great Desert. El-Jereed is identified as the Tunisian Sahara, while most of the broader region between the Atlantic and Egypt is known among Arabs as the Sahara or Sahra.

l: El-Sibhah, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: El-Sibhah, literally the salt plain, is a vast salt lake in El-Jereed. It extends about seventy English miles from north-east to south-west and contains dry areas whose number and extent vary with the season. Its salt is weaker than sea salt, has an agreeable flavour, and is not exported or used commercially.

l: dates, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Dates are the principal food and resource of El-Jereed. They are stored in bunches suspended from poles and pressed into large earthen jars, where their juice collects as a thick syrup. They may also be dried and ground into meal that keeps indefinitely and serves as a valuable food for desert travellers.

l: date-palm, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The date-palm is male and female, and the female requires communication with the male to produce good fruit. Trees propagated from shoots can bear in six or seven years, while those grown from stones require sixteen years; according to Tunisian accounts, they reach greatest vigour at about thirty years and may bear for seventy years. The palm also supplies sap, fruit, leaves, fibres, wood, baskets, ropes, and other useful materials.

l: palm-groves, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Palm-groves are described as beautiful plantations whose trees are generally planted in a quincunx or at distances of four or five yards apart. They are commonly situated beside streams or rivulets, and abundant water produces healthier trees and finer fruit. The groves may yield very large quantities of dates, with one plantation producing fifteen hundred camels' loads.

l: irrigation, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Irrigation is essential to the date-palm and is carried out in spring and throughout the summer. Small channels carry water from a stream to basins formed around individual trees, where clay embankments hold the water until it soaks into the earth. The palms tolerate water that is salt, sweet, or impregnated with nitre.

l: date cultivation, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Date cultivation requires regular watering at the roots every four or five days and the removal of lower branches when they droop or wither. The palms are usually propagated from shoots, and the male plants are hung or shaken over the female plants in February or March to ensure fruitfulness. Excessive rain injures the dates, although the trees thrive in generally dry countries.

l: date trade, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Dates are exported from El-Jereed to other parts of the Regency and to foreign countries because of their fine quality. The average annual export is stated as three to four thousand quintals. The produce of a large plantation may be sold for one thousand dollars.

l: tribute collection, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Tribute collection is one of the duties associated with governing El-Jereed and the other divisions of the Regency. It is carried out through a yearly visit by a flying camp led by the Bey of the Camp.

l: Bey of the Camp, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Bey of the Camp visits El-Jereed each year with a flying camp to administer affairs and collect tribute. He is described as sovereign in the country and as heir-apparent to the Tunisian throne. On the death of the reigning Bey, he occupies the hereditary beylick and nominates his successor, generally according to seniority within the royal family.

l: Tour to the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Tour to the Jereed is introduced as a narrative extracted from the tourists' notebooks and supplemented with the author's observations. It is intended to provide further details about the region, including Toser, Nefta, and Ghafsa.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: Captain Balfour and Richard Reade joined Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, on an expedition through the Jereed toward Kairwan. The Bey's camp included Mamelukes, Turkish Infantry, Spahis, Arab camp followers, artillery, attendants, and water-carriers, and followed a formal daily order of march. The tourists observed Tunisian customs, justice, saints' shrines, poor water supplies, ruined bridges, and the severe-looking but often merely formal bastinado. They also hunted partridges, hares, gazelles, wild boar, foxes, wolves, and hyaenas across plains and hills.

l: Captain B., Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: Captain Balfour joined the tour through the Jereed with Richard Reade. A wad from a ceremonial gun nearly struck him on the head, and he later hunted with the Bey's doctor and observed the Turkish Infantry and the camp's daily movements.

l: R., Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: Richard Reade joined Captain Balfour on the expedition and received the skin and head of a hyaena, along with a fine bay horse, as presents from the Bey. He reported that Sidi Mohammed was an exceptionally accurate shot from horseback.

l: Sidi Mohammed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, led the expedition from the Bardo across the plain of Manouba toward the Jereed. He regularly paid respects at saints' shrines, hunted daily, saluted the various divisions of the march, received local officers, and treated the tourists with familiarity and kindness.

l: Mr. Reade, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: The tourists traveled with the Bey's expedition, carrying their baggage on three camels and staying in a tent near the Bey's. They visited the Bey, observed the camp's organization and customs, hunted extensively, and received his presents and hospitality.

l: the expedition and camp, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Bey's camp contained about 2,660 men, including Mamelukes, Turkish Infantry, Spahis, and Arab camp followers, as well as two artillery pieces. Its tents were arranged around the Bey's central tent, and its attendants included guards of the pipe, gun, coffee, shoes, and water, together with a story-teller and a supply of water brought from Tunis.

l: Turkish Infantry, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: The 300 Turkish Infantry followed the mounted troops by about two hours and were honored by the Bey when they caught up. They were described as highly irregular, performed sham sword fights and music for the Bey, guarded the camp at night, and repeatedly shouted 'Alleya.'

l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: Arab troops and camp followers formed most of the expedition's supporting force, and additional Arab groups joined temporarily as honorary welcomes to the Bey. Arabs were described as eating dogs, foxes, wolves, and other animals, while some were flogged for stealing barley; Arab women saluted the passing camp with shrill looloos.

l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: The tourists began their journey from Tunis and sent baggage to Giovanni, the 'Guarda-pipa.' Water for the Bey was carried from Tunis by camels, and the tourists returned there briefly to obtain neglected supplies before rejoining the expedition.

l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Jereed was the destination of Sidi Mohammed's expedition with Captain Balfour and Richard Reade. It was portrayed as a largely flat, dry region with sparse inhabitants, little water, ruins, Arab encampments, and extensive plains suitable for hunting.

l: the plain of Manouba, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Bey crossed the plain of Manouba after leaving the Bardo. It was covered by baggage-camels, horses, mules, attendants, and troops moving in what the tourists called glorious confusion.
